![Image from [Stratechery](https://stratechery.com/2026/the-inference-shift/).](cover.jpg){fig-align="center"}

[Ben Thompson](https://stratechery.com/about/) uses the [Cerebras](https://www.cerebras.ai/) IPO as a hook to [argue](https://stratechery.com/2026/the-inference-shift/) that what the industry has been calling "inference" is actually two workloads with very different hardware implications:

- ***Answer inference*** is what a human waits on. Token speed matters, so bandwidth-rich chips (GPUs with [high-bandwidth memory (HBM)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Bandwidth_Memory), or wafer-scale designs like [Cerebras' WSE-3](https://www.cerebras.ai/chip)) win.
- ***Agentic inference*** is what a computer waits on. With no human in the loop, latency is cheap and memory capacity is everything. The model sits inside a hierarchy of [key-value (KV) cache](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/kv_cache), DRAM, SSDs, databases, and embeddings, and "good enough" compute wrapped in lots of cheap memory beats high-bandwidth compute starved for context.

If agentic inference becomes the largest market by far because it scales with compute rather than with humans, Nvidia's price advantage, earned on latency, gets less valuable exactly where the volume lives. China, which cannot buy the leading edge for training, already has everything it needs for agentic inference. Space data centers start to make sense too, because older, slower nodes tolerate radiation and dissipate less heat. Thompson ends by inverting his usual Huang-era stance: "Moore's Law doesn't matter, and that the way we get more compute is by realizing that the compute we have is already good enough."

## My Notes

- **The price premium on this hardware comes from latency, and workloads where no human is waiting eventually migrate off it. Thompson is arguing that's what's about to happen to agentic inference.**
  - Mainframes in the 1970s ran two workloads on the same expensive hardware: interactive timesharing (a human at a terminal is waiting, latency-sensitive, what the premium was really justified by) and batch jobs (no human is waiting, latency-tolerant, the premium going unused).
  - Machine-time cost collapsed by orders of magnitude over this period; human-time cost moved slowly by comparison. The end of the mainframe monopoly was driven by commodity compute getting cheaper on two fronts at once: batch workloads migrated to cheaper shared servers (minicomputer-class, then Unix workstations, then commodity x86 clusters), and interactive computing migrated to per-user PCs. Mainframes survived in domains where the premium is genuinely justified (banks, airlines, reservation systems), but they stopped being the volume market.
  - Thompson's answer-inference vs. agentic-inference split is the same split on today's GPU clusters. Answer inference is the interactive tier: a human is waiting, the latency premium is justified. Agentic inference is the batch tier: no human is waiting, latency is free, the GPU's premium characteristics are going unused. Once agentic workloads are large enough, they migrate off the premium tier onto a commodity memory hierarchy, the way batch unbundled from the mainframe.
  - The mapping:

    | Era | Dominant "user" | Interactive tier | Batch tier | Hardware shape |
    |---|---|---|---|---|
    | Mainframe (1970s) | Humans | Timesharing | Overnight batch | Integrated premium iron |
    | PC (1980s–2010s) | Humans | Desktop | Cluster/server batch | Commodity, unbundled, per-user |
    | Current AI (2022–2026) | Humans | Chat / autocomplete | "Agent runs" on the same GPUs | Integrated premium GPUs; answer tier has colonized the batch tier |
    | Agentic shift | Agents | Answer inference (stays premium) | Agentic inference | Answer tier stays integrated; agentic tier unbundles into a commodity memory hierarchy |

  - The prediction that falls out: Nvidia keeps the training-and-answer-inference premium (the pieces where human time is still on the clock) and cedes the volume market, the way IBM kept mainframes and ceded personal computing. Export-control arbitrage rhymes too: Cold-War restrictions on leading-edge systems stopped tracking the market once PC-class compute proliferated.

- **The memory hierarchy is where the money actually goes.** Thompson's phrasing, "the memory hierarchy wrapped around a model," describes agentic systems as mostly a storage-and-retrieval problem with a language model as one stage in the pipeline, rather than as "a GPU answering a question." If he's right about the economics, a lot of the investment that today goes into more HBM per card gets redirected down the hierarchy, into DRAM, SSDs, and the databases and stores that actually hold the agent's state.

- **The 220,000 Nvidia GPUs Anthropic just contracted at Colossus 1 are the shape of the locked-in bet.** That's latency-first hardware on a decade-long depreciation schedule. [Anthropic's own announcement](https://www.anthropic.com/news/higher-limits-spacex) earmarks the capacity for Claude Pro and Max subscribers: a mix of answer inference and agent runs on the same clusters today. Thompson's argument implies the agent portion of that mix will grow faster than the answer portion, and increasingly won't need what the fleet is optimized for. Hyperscalers with similar high-end-GPU-dense fleets face the same exposure. A year of elevated Nvidia prices was always the smaller concern; the larger one is whether the fleet's shape matches the workload mix for the next depreciation cycle.

- **Two prior posts are worth tying back here.** In 2020 the open question around [Huang's Law](/posts/20200920-huangs-law-gpt3/) was whether Nvidia's exponential curve would democratize big models; Thompson is now arguing the interesting frontier may not sit on that curve at all. At a meta level the piece also echoes the mechanism in the [2028 Global Intelligence Crisis scenario](/posts/20260502-2028-intelligence-crisis/): once humans stop being the anchor for how much compute can get used, the old "paid human time" ceiling disappears, whether the effect shows up as expanding agentic markets here or as labor substitution there.
